claim: Elevated levels of alpha-synuclein (α-Syn) appear to drive neurotoxicity in Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: Elevated levels of alpha-synuclein (α-Syn) appear to drive neurotoxicity in Parkinson's disease (PD)
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established understanding in the field, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: Neuronal accumulation of tau is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: neuronal accumulation of tau is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD)
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of neurodegenerative disease research.

claim: Increased levels of α-Syn and tau cause neurodegeneration in humans and model organisms.
source: their increased levels cause neurodegeneration in humans and model organisms
evidence: This statement is supported by references to established scientific knowledge about proteinopathies.

claim: α-Syn and tau overlap pathologically despite clinical differences between AD and PD.
source: Despite the clinical differences between AD and PD, several lines of evidence suggest that α-Syn and tau overlap pathologically.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from multiple lines of evidence mentioned in the introduction.

claim: TRIM28 regulates α-Syn and tau levels.
source: We found that TRIM28 regulates α-Syn and tau levels
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the screens and validation experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Reduction of TRIM28 rescues toxicity in animal models of tau- and α-Syn-mediated degeneration.
source: its reduction rescues toxicity in animal models of tau- and α-Syn-mediated degeneration
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Drosophila and mouse models shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: TRIM28 stabilizes and promotes the nuclear accumulation and toxicity of both α-Syn and tau.
source: TRIM28 stabilizes and promotes the nuclear accumulation and toxicity of both proteins.
evidence: This is supported by protein stability assays (Figure 5), nuclear localization studies (Figure 6), and toxicity experiments (Figures 2-4).

claim: α-Syn mediates neurotoxicity in Parkinson's Disease Dementia (PDD) and Lewy Body Dementia (LBD) where it accumulates in Lewy bodies.
source: alpha-synuclein (α-Syn, SNCA) is now thought to mediate neurotoxicity not only in Parkinson's disease (PD), but also in Parkinson's Disease Dementia (PDD) and Lewy Body Dementia (LBD) where it accumulates in Lewy bodies (Spillantini et al., 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spillantini et al., 1997.

claim: Tau accumulates in neurons affected by Alzheimer's disease (AD), PD, and PDD.
source: the microtubule associated protein tau (MAPT) accumulates not only in neurons affected by Alzheimer's disease (AD), but in PD and PDD
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field of neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Mutations that increase the stability of tau result in frontotemporal dementia with parkinsonism (FTDP-17 or FTD).
source: while mutations that increase the stability of tau result in frontotemporal dementia with parkinsonism (FTDP-17 (or FTD) [Spillantini and Goedert, 2013])
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spillantini and Goedert, 2013.

claim: Duplication or triplication of the SNCA locus is sufficient to result in forms of PD whose onset and severity correlate with gene dosage.
source: duplication or triplication of the SNCA locus is sufficient to result in forms of PD whose onset and severity correlate with gene dosage (Chartier-Harlin et al., 2004; Ibanez et al., 2004; Singleton, 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies: Chartier-Harlin et al., 2004; Ibanez et al., 2004; Singleton, 2003.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type forms of either SNCA or MAPT elicit neurodegeneration in model organisms.
source: studies that show that overexpression of wild-type forms of either SNCA or MAPT elicit neurodegeneration in model organisms, whereas suppressing their levels appears to be neuroprotective (Dauer et al., 2002; Ishihara et al., 1999; Jackson et al., 2002; Rapoport et al., 2002; Rockenstein et al., 2002; Wittmann, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Dauer et al., 2002; Ishihara et al., 1999; Jackson et al., 2002; Rapoport et al., 2002; Rockenstein et al., 2002; Wittmann, 2001.

claim: Suppressing levels of SNCA or MAPT appears to be neuroprotective.
source: whereas suppressing their levels appears to be neuroprotective (Dauer et al., 2002; Ishihara et al., 1999; Jackson et al., 2002; Rapoport et al., 2002; Rockenstein et al., 2002; Wittmann, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Dauer et al., 2002; Ishihara et al., 1999; Jackson et al., 2002; Rapoport et al., 2002; Rockenstein et al., 2002; Wittmann, 2001.

claim: Elevated levels of multiple proteins (α-Syn and tau) are more problematic than elevated levels of a single protein.
source: one would expect elevated levels of multiple proteins to be even more problematic, and this proves to be the case (Moussaud et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moussaud et al., 2014.

claim: Pathogenic proteins involved in different proteinopathies often interact with each other and cause cellular toxicity.
source: Pathogenic proteins involved in different proteionopathies often interact with each other and cause cellular toxicity, either due to their additive effects on downstream activities or further compromise of protein homeostasis (Clinton et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clinton et al., 2010.

claim: Abnormally aggregated α-Syn and tau are often found together in postmortem cases of PD and LBD.
source: Abnormally aggregated α-Syn and tau are often found together in postmortem cases of PD and LBD (Arima et al., 1999; Colom-Cadena et al., 2013; Iseki et al., 2002; Ishizawa et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four studies: Arima et al., 1999; Colom-Cadena et al., 2013; Iseki et al., 2002; Ishizawa et al., 2003.

claim: α-Syn and tau synergize in promoting toxicity in Drosophila.
source: genetic interaction studies in Drosophila demonstrate that α-Syn and tau synergize in promoting toxicity (Roy and Jackson, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roy and Jackson, 2014.

claim: α-Syn may act as an amyloidogenic 'seed' for the accumulation of tau, and vice versa.
source: Biochemical evidence even suggests that α-Syn may act as an amyloidogenic 'seed' for the accumulation of tau, and vice versa (Guo et al., 2013; Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2010; Sengupta et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies: Guo et al., 2013; Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2010; Sengupta et al., 2015.

claim: Several genome-wide association studies have reported genetic interaction between tau and alpha-synuclein in PD pathogenesis.
source: several genome-wide association studies have reported genetic interaction between tau and alpha-synuclein in PD pathogenesis (Simón-Sánchez et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Simón-Sánchez et al., 2009.

claim: The mechanisms governing the dual accumulation of α-Syn and tau remain elusive.
source: The mechanisms governing the dual accumulation of α-Syn and tau remain elusive
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Decreasing levels of either or both α-Syn and tau could prove an effective therapeutic strategy for proteinopathies.
source: it seems plausible that decreasing levels of either or both of these proteins could prove an effective therapeutic strategy for this family of diseases
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the evidence presented about protein accumulation and toxicity.

claim: The screening strategy employed was similar to one recently used to identify key modulators of ATXN1 stability.
source: We employed a screening strategy similar to one recently used to identify key modulators of ATXN1 stability (Park et al., 2013; Westbrook et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2013 and Westbrook et al., 2008.

claim: The screen interrogated 2607 siRNAs targeting 869 potentially druggable genes.
source: We ran parallel screens interrogating 2607 siRNAs targeting 869 potentially druggable – i.e. potentially can be targeted pharmacologically – genes to identify genes that modify the levels of both α-Syn and tau (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C and Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design described in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: TRIM28 was identified as the most robust common modulator of α-Syn and tau levels.
source: we uncovered Tripartite motif-containing 28 (TRIM28) as the most robust common modulator (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by the screening data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Three independent siRNAs against TRIM28 confirmed its effect on α-Syn and tau stability.
source: We confirmed this effect of TRIM28 knock-down on α-Syn and tau stability using three independent siRNAs on our α-Syn and tau reporter cell lines along with a negative control cell line (DsRed-IRES-EGFP) to ensure that TRIM28 was not affecting the stability of EGFP (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Partial reduction of TRIM28 led to a decrease of both α-Syn and tau in human cells, mouse primary cerebellar neurons, and mouse hippocampus.
source: In each case, partial reduction of TRIM28 led to a decrease of both α-Syn and tau
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Virally reintroducing a human shRNA-resistant TRIM28 cDNA reversed the effect of TRIM28 knockdown on α-Syn and tau levels.
source: virally reintroducing a human shRNA-resistant TRIM28 cDNA reversed this effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Deleting one allele of Trim28 in mice led to a modest but significant decrease of α-Syn and tau levels in mouse brain.
source: we found that deleting one allele of Trim28 in mice led to a modest but significant decrease of α-Syn and tau levels in mouse brain (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: TRIM28 downregulation resulted in little to no changes in SNCA nor MAPT transcript levels.
source: we observed little to no changes in SNCA nor MAPT transcript levels under conditions of TRIM28 downregulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D)
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Reduction of TRIM28 did not affect other neurodegeneration-causing proteins tested.
source: Nor did reduction of TRIM28 affect other neurodegeneration-causing proteins we tested (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: TRIM28 is a key post-translational regulator of the steady state levels of α-Syn and tau.
source: TRIM28 thus appears to be a key post-translational regulator of the steady state levels of α-Syn and tau
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing TRIM28 affects protein but not RNA levels.

claim: Knockdown of the Drosophila TRIM28 homolog (bonus) significantly reduced tau levels and mitigated eye degeneration in tau-expressing flies.
source: Knockdown of the Drosophila TRIM28 homolog (bonus) significantly reduced tau levels and mitigated eye degeneration (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Two independent partial loss-of-function alleles of TRIM28 improved motor deficits in tau-expressing Drosophila without reducing transgene expression.
source: two independent partial loss-of-function alleles of TRIM28 improved this behavioral phenotype without reducing the transgene expression (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Video 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: Reduction of TRIM28 effectively decreased tau levels in Drosophila.
source: we tested the effect of TRIM28 loss of function on transgenic tau levels and found indeed that reduction of TRIM28 could effectively decrease tau levels in this heterologous system (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mice infected with viruses overexpressing α-Syn and a control shRNA suffered a 50% reduction in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive dopaminergic neurons.
source: Mice infected with viruses overexpressing α-Syn and a control shRNA suffered a 50% reduction in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive dopaminergic neurons (Figure 3A,B-top panels and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mice that received the shTrim28 virus together with α-Syn overexpression maintained their dopaminergic cells in the SNc and the corresponding fibers in the striatum.
source: mice that received the shTrim28 virus together with α-Syn overexpression maintained their dopaminergic cells in the SNc and the corresponding fibers in the striatum (Figure 3A,B-bottom panels)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: A 50% reduction in Trim28 significantly reduced pathological, phosphorylated α-Syn accumulation in the hippocampus of α-Syn-overexpressing mice.
source: We found that a 50% reduction in Trim28 significantly reduced pathological, phosphorylated α-Syn accumulation in the hippocampus where it is highly expressed (Figure 3C,D) (Chesselet et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D, with a citation to Chesselet et al., 2012.

claim: Bilateral lentiviral overexpression of TRIM28 in pre-symptomatic mouse models of synucleinopathy and tauopathy worsened each aspect of neuropathology tested.
source: We performed bilateral lentiviral overexpression of TRIM28 in pre-symptomatic mouse models of synucleinopathy (Rockenstein et al., 2002) and tauopathy (Yoshiyama et al., 2007) and found that injection with TRIM28, but not control lentivirus, worsened each aspect of neuropathology tested in both models (Figure 4A,B; and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B, with citations to Rockenstein et al., 2002 and Yoshiyama et al., 2007.

claim: TRIM28 lentiviral overexpression significantly increased the half-life of α-Syn and tau by approximately 50%.
source: we found that TRIM28 lentiviral overexpression could significantly increase the half-life of each protein by approximately 50% (LV-TRIM28 vs. LV-Ctrl, Figure 5B,C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: TRIM28 overexpression did not affect the RNA stability of α-Syn and tau.
source: without affecting their RNA stability (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRIM28 promotes the accumulation of the amyloidogenic proteins α-Syn and tau.
source: these studies suggest that TRIM28 promotes the accumulation of the amyloidogenic proteins α-Syn and tau
evidence: This is an inference based on the stability and overexpression data.

claim: TRIM28 interacts with α-Syn and tau, albeit weakly, in human cells.
source: We asked whether TRIM28 modulates α-Syn and tau by forming a complex with them and found that they did indeed interact, albeit weakly, in human cells (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TRIM28:α-Syn and TRIM28:tau complexes accumulated in nuclei after some time as shown by BiFC assay.
source: Intriguingly, TRIM28:α-Syn and TRIM28:tau complexes accumulated in nuclei after some time
evidence: This is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Viral expression of TRIM28 dramatically promoted the nuclear accumulation of α-Syn and tau in primary cerebellar granule neurons.
source: we found that viral expression of TRIM28 dramatically promoted the nuclear accumulation of these two proteins (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: An inactive TRIM28 E3 ligase mutant (C65A/C68A) could no longer promote the toxic nuclear accumulation of α-Syn and tau.
source: We overexpressed an inactive TRIM28 E3 ligase mutant ([C65A/C68A], 'TRIM28-Mut') (Doyle et al., 2010) and found that this mutant could no longer promote the toxic nuclear accumulation of these proteins (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, with a citation to Doyle et al., 2010.

claim: The TRIM28 E3 ligase mutant could still bind α-Syn and tau, though less stably.
source: we found that the TRIM28 E3 ligase mutant, while less stable, could still bind α-Syn and tau (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: TRIM28 governs the nuclear accumulation of α-Syn and tau through its E3-ligase domain.
source: TRIM28 governs the nuclear accumulation of α-Syn and tau through its E3-ligase domain
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant data showing that the E3 ligase activity is required for nuclear accumulation.

claim: Persistent expression of TRIM28 aggravates the neuropathology of both α-Syn and tau.
source: its persistent expression aggravates the neuropathology of both proteins
evidence: This is supported by the overexpression data in mouse models shown in Figure 4.

claim: In all cases of synucleinopathy and tauopathy, a greater proportion of TRIM28 accumulated in an insoluble form (Formic Acid fraction) than the more soluble form (RIPA fraction).
source: In all cases of synucleinopathy and tauopathy, a greater proportion of TRIM28 accumulated in an insoluble form (Formic Acid fraction) than the more soluble form (RIPA fraction) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: This is supported by biochemical fractionation data from human postmortem tissue shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: α-Syn and tau accumulated in the nucleus in most cases of synucleinopathy and tauopathy.
source: Subcellular fractionation on these post-mortem tissues revealed that α-Syn and tau accumulated in the nucleus in most cases of synucleinopathy and tauopathy (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B)
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data from human postmortem tissue shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: α-Syn and tau nuclear co-localization with TRIM28 was greater in PD and AD than in age-matched controls.
source: We found that α-Syn and tau nuclear co-localization with TRIM28 was greater in PD and AD than in age-matched controls (Figure 7A,B)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data from human postmortem tissue shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: TRIM28 is aberrantly increased in cases of synucleinopathy and tauopathy.
source: our findings suggest that TRIM28 is aberrantly increased in cases of synucleinopathy and tauopathy
evidence: This is an inference based on the biochemical fractionation data showing increased insoluble TRIM28 in disease cases.

claim: Altered cellular distribution of α-Syn and tau contributes to neurodegeneration.
source: Our finding that TRIM28 regulates α-Syn and tau by promoting their nuclear localization and accumulation dovetails nicely with studies indicating that altered cellular distribution of α-Syn and tau contributes to neurodegeneration (Fares et al., 2014; Fernández-Nogales et al., 2014; Kontopoulos et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fares et al., 2014; Fernández-Nogales et al., 2014; Kontopoulos et al., 2006.

claim: Mislocalization or missorting of α-Syn and tau, rather than their respective aggregation in the form of Lewy bodies and NFTs, promotes neurodegeneration.
source: several lines of evidence suggest that mislocalization or missorting of α-Syn and tau as a result of mutations, post-translational modification or overexpression, rather than their respective aggregation in the form of Lewy bodies and NFTs, are what promotes neurodegeneration (Frandemiche et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Frandemiche et al., 2014 and Wilson et al., 2004.

claim: α-Syn is much more toxic in a fly model of synucleinopathy when it is tagged with a nuclear localization sequence (NLS).
source: α-Syn is much more toxic in a fly model of synucleinopathy when it is tagged with a nuclear localization sequence (NLS) (Kontopoulos et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kontopoulos et al., 2006.

claim: PD-causing mutations in α-Syn increase its nuclear accumulation.
source: PD-causing mutations in α-Syn increase its nuclear accumulation (Fares et al., 2014; Kontopoulos et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fares et al., 2014 and Kontopoulos et al., 2006.

claim: Postmortem studies of tissue from AD and Huntington disease patients indicate that misfolded tau accumulates in the nucleus of neurons in the form of rod-like deposits.
source: postmortem studies of tissue from AD and Huntington disease patients indicate that misfolded tau accumulates in the nucleus of neurons in the form of rod-like deposits (Fernández-Nogales et al., 2014; Vuono et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fernández-Nogales et al., 2014 and Vuono et al., 2015.

claim: TRIM28 drives the nuclear accumulation of α-Syn and tau, providing new mechanistic insight into the steps that lead to the pathogenicity of these proteins.
source: Our finding that TRIM28 drives the nuclear accumulation of α-Syn and tau provides new mechanistic insight into the steps that lead to the pathogenicity of these proteins
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing TRIM28's role in nuclear accumulation.

claim: The Trim28 null mice are embryonic lethal.
source: While the Trim28 null mice are embryonic lethal (Cammas et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cammas et al., 2000.

claim: Trim28+/- mice looked and behaved normally.
source: we found that the Trim28+/- mice looked and behaved normally
evidence: This is based on observations from the study.

claim: 50% loss of Trim28 was sufficient to reduce α-Syn and tau and ameliorate toxicity.
source: 50% loss of Trim28 was sufficient to reduce α-Syn and tau and ameliorate toxicity
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Trim28+/- mice shown in Figure 1C and Figure 3C, D.

claim: Mutating the E3 ligase catalytic activity of TRIM28 is sufficient to regulate α-Syn and tau levels and behaves like a null allele for this specific effect.
source: having discovered that mutating the E3 ligase catalytic activity of TRIM28 effectively is sufficient to regulate α-Syn and tau levels and for this specific effect behaves like a null allele
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing the E3 ligase mutant cannot promote nuclear accumulation.

claim: The overlap of 41 genes between α-Syn and tau screens is statistically significant (p=9.5 × 10–4).
source: In A, p=9.5 × 10–4, hypergeometric test
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the screen overlap shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The half-life of α-Syn in the doxycycline-inducible system is 23.3 hours.
source: We found that the half-lives of α-Syn and tau (measured following a 48 hr pulse of doxycycline) in this system resembled those previously observed by others (23.3 hr for α-Syn and 28.1 hr for tau [Li, 2004; Min et al., 2010])
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the stability assay, with citations to Li, 2004 and Min et al., 2010.

claim: The half-life of tau in the doxycycline-inducible system is 28.1 hours.
source: We found that the half-lives of α-Syn and tau (measured following a 48 hr pulse of doxycycline) in this system resembled those previously observed by others (23.3 hr for α-Syn and 28.1 hr for tau [Li, 2004; Min et al., 2010])
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the stability assay, with citations to Li, 2004 and Min et al., 2010.
